title: Weak point Wednesday: Lats (how I will grow mine)
summary: First Weak Point Wednesday episode: he explains why his lats lagged (relying on deadlifts, rows and machine pulldowns) and how they finally started growing via very high frequency pull-ups, wide-grip Pendlay rows, Coan/cheat rows for the stretch, and pullovers. He prefers free-weight vertical pulls over machines and avoids supinated Yates rows for biceps safety.

claims.claim: He long believed he had high lat insertions and bad genetics, but that was a cope; his lats are now growing fast and are very vascular.
The meme that you only need deadlifts and rows to grow lats is wrong; his lats didn't grow from them.
With machines, a strong middle back takes over and you pull with it rather than the lats, given the machine's moment arm.
Many cable machines seat you far from the pull point, so you pull in front of you and never reach the lat stretch you get hanging under a pull-up bar with the bar in line with the collarbones.

For him, wide overhand pull-ups work the lats best, then wide neutral grip, then wide supinated; close grips hit his mid back more because he is narrow, except close supinated chin-ups, where he feels his lats.
He does pull-ups every day: about 100-120 bodyweight pull-ups on high-volume days and 30-40 on lower-volume days.
Pull-ups done with the back don't touch the CNS, shouldn't hurt wrists, elbows or shoulders, and the upper back recovers very fast, which allows daily frequency.
Lats get sore but it never lasts; they're always ready to work.
He has never heard of a natural tearing a lat; like quad tears, it's an injury he associates with PED users.

He used to Pendlay row 235-245 lbs with a normal grip and never felt his lats, only rear delts and traps; switching to a wide (snatch) grip, touching the sternum and arching the lower back made him feel his lats much more with less weight.
Pendlay rows have no stretch at the bottom, and the stretch is very important for lats.
His bread-and-butter heavy lat movement is Coan (cheat) rows with very heavy weight, letting the bar stretch the back at the bottom.
He does many light dumbbell pullovers (30 lbs) focusing on the lat connection and stretch, alternating volume with pull-ups: fewer pull-ups means more pullovers and vice versa.
He has a much better mind-muscle connection with his right lat than his left and adjusts hand position on the dumbbell to work around it.
One day a week he goes heavy on dumbbell pullovers: 60 lbs for about 12 reps per set, 50-60 total reps.
He uses no machines or pulldowns for lats.

He thinks the Yates row is the best lat hypertrophy movement, but hitting the lower lats requires a supinated grip with a stretch at the bottom, which he won't risk because the biceps are far less resilient than the upper back and would give first.
He considers supinated-grip rows unsafe and is looking for an overhand Yates row angle that still hits the lats.
